```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(kableExtra)
library(openxlsx)

# Actual home repo
home = stringr::str_remove(getwd(), "/Reports")

# ORA and GSEA pathway tables
pathways <- list(
  "Gene Ontology" = "Gene Ontology.xlsx",
  "KEGG" = "KEGG.xlsx",
  "WikiPathways" = "WikiPathways.xlsx",
  "Reactome" = "Reactome.xlsx",
  "Disease Ontology" = "Disease Ontology.xlsx",
  "Network of Cancer Gene (NCG)" = "Network Cancer Gene (NCG).xlsx",
  "Disease Gene Network (DisGeNET)" = "Disease Gene Network (DisGeNET).xlsx"
)

# pathfindR pathway tables
pathfindR_pathways = c("GO-BP", "GO-MF", "GO-CC", "Reactome", "KEGG", "BioCarta")

# Automated functions ###
# ORA loop
ora_loop = function(ora_pathways, comp = NULL) {
  for (pathway in names(ora_pathways)) {
    file_name <- ora_pathways[[pathway]]
    
    file_path <- file.path(home, "Results", "Pathways", comp, "ORA", paste0("top_ORA_output_", comp, "_", pathway, ".xlsx"))
    
    # Check if the file exists and has at least one row
    if (file.exists(file_path) && nrow(read.xlsx(file_path)) > 0) {
      # Create the collapsible details section
      cat(paste0("<details>\n    <summary>", pathway, "</summary>\n\n"))
      
      # Read the Excel file
      top10max <- read.xlsx(file_path)
      
      # Generate the table
      table <- kable(top10max, 
                     caption = paste("Top Significant", pathway, "ORA Results"), 
                     format = "html", 
                     escape = FALSE) %>%
        kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "center")
      
      # Apply column_spec based on column names
      if ("Description" %in% colnames(top10max)) {
        desc_col <- which(colnames(top10max) == "Description")
        table <- table %>% column_spec(desc_col, width = "200px")
      }
      
      if ("geneID" %in% colnames(top10max)) {
        geneID_col <- which(colnames(top10max) == "geneID")
        table <- table %>% column_spec(geneID_col, width = "300px")
      }
      
      # Print the table
      print(table)
      
      # Close the details tag
      cat("</details>\n\n")
    }
  }
}

# pathfindR
pathfindR_loop = function(pathfindR_pathways, comp = NULL) {
  for (pathway in pathfindR_pathways) {
    file_name <- pathways[[pathway]]
    comprehensive_file_path <- file.path(home, "Results", "Pathways", comp, "pathfindR", paste0("top_Comprehensive_pathfindR_output_", pathway, ".xlsx"))
    representative_file_path <- file.path(home, "Results", "Pathways", comp, "pathfindR", paste0("top_Representative_pathfindR_output_", pathway, ".xlsx"))
  
    # Check if the file exists and has at least one row
    if (file.exists(comprehensive_file_path) && nrow(read.xlsx(comprehensive_file_path)) > 0) {
      # Create the collapsible details section
      cat(paste0("<details>\n    <summary>Comprehensive ", pathway, " Results</summary>\n\n"))
    
      # Read the Excel file
      top10max <- read.xlsx(comprehensive_file_path)
    
      # Generate the table
      table <- kable(top10max, 
                     caption = paste("Top Significant", pathway, "pathfindR Results (All terms)"), 
                     format = "html", 
                     escape = FALSE) %>%
        kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "center")
    
      # Apply column_spec based on column names
      if ("Description" %in% colnames(top10max)) {
        desc_col <- which(colnames(top10max) == "Description")
        table <- table %>% column_spec(desc_col, width = "200px")
      }
    
      if ("Up-regulated" %in% colnames(top10max)) {
        ur_col <- which(colnames(top10max) == "Up-regulated")
        table <- table %>% column_spec(ur_col, width = "150px")
      }
    
      if ("Down-regulated" %in% colnames(top10max)) {
        dr_col <- which(colnames(top10max) == "Down-regulated")
        table <- table %>% column_spec(dr_col, width = "150px")
      }
    
      # Print the table
      print(table)
    
      # Close the details tag
      cat("</details>\n\n")
    }
  
    # Check if the file exists and has at least one row
    if (file.exists(representative_file_path) && nrow(read.xlsx(representative_file_path)) > 0) {
      # Create the collapsible details section
      cat(paste0("<details>\n    <summary>Representative ", pathway, " Results</summary>\n\n"))
    
      # Read the Excel file
      top10max <- read.xlsx(representative_file_path)
    
      # Generate the table
      table <- kable(top10max, 
                     caption = paste("Top Significant", pathway, "pathfindR Results (Representative terms)"), 
                     format = "html", 
                     escape = FALSE) %>%
        kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "center")
    
      # Apply column_spec based on column names
      if ("Description" %in% colnames(top10max)) {
        desc_col <- which(colnames(top10max) == "Description")
        table <- table %>% column_spec(desc_col, width = "200px")
      }
    
      if ("Up-regulated" %in% colnames(top10max)) {
        ur_col <- which(colnames(top10max) == "Up-regulated")
        table <- table %>% column_spec(ur_col, width = "150px")
      }
    
      if ("Down-regulated" %in% colnames(top10max)) {
        dr_col <- which(colnames(top10max) == "Down-regulated")
        table <- table %>% column_spec(dr_col, width = "150px")
      }
    
      # Print the table
      print(table)
    
      # Close the details tag
      cat("</details>\n\n")
    }
  }
}

pathfindR_plot_loops = function (pathfindR_pathways, comp = NULL, exclude = c()) {
  for (pathway in pathfindR_pathways) {
    if (pathway %in% exclude) {
      next
    } else {
      file_name <- pathways[[pathway]]
      file_path1 <- file.path(home, "Reports", "png_pathways", comp, pathway, paste0(pathway, "_top10_term_gene_heatmap.png"))
      file_path2 <- file.path(home, "Reports", "png_pathways", comp, pathway, paste0(pathway, "_top10_dotplot.png"))
      file_path3 <- file.path(home, "Reports", "png_pathways", comp, pathway, paste0(pathway, "_top10_dotplot_clustered.png"))
      file_path4 <- file.path(home, "Reports", "png_pathways", comp, pathway, paste0(pathway, "_per_sample_pathway_scores_clustered.png"))
      
      # Initiate section per set
      cat(paste0("<details>\n    <summary>", pathway, "</summary>\n\n"))
      if (file.exists(file_path1)) {
        cat(paste0("<details>\n",
             "  <summary>", pathway, " Term-Gene heatmap</summary>\n\n",
             "  ![](", file_path1, ")\n\n",
             "</details>\n\n"))
      }
      if (file.exists(file_path2)) {
        cat(paste0("<details>\n",
             "  <summary>", pathway, " Dot plot</summary>\n\n",
             "  ![](", file_path2, ")\n\n",
             "</details>\n\n"))
      }
      if (file.exists(file_path3)) {
        cat(paste0("<details>\n",
             "  <summary>", pathway, " Representative Dot plot</summary>\n\n",
             "  ![](", file_path3, ")\n\n",
             "</details>\n\n"))
      }
      if (file.exists(file_path4)) {
        cat(paste0("<details>\n",
             "  <summary>", pathway, " Per-Sample Pathway Scores</summary>\n\n",
             "  ![](", file_path4, ")\n\n",
             "</details>\n\n"))
      }
      
      # Close the section
      cat("</details>\n\n")
    }
  }
}
```

# Overview
<b> Overview of the analysis steps: </b>
<ol>
  <li>Upload raw sequences in [Kraken2](https://ccb.jhu.edu/software/kraken2/) for examining taxonomy issues.</li>
  <li>Run the <b>nextflow</b> [nf-core rnaseq](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.14.0/) pipeline with default parameters on the Aristotle HPC cluster (<b>for single-end, NOT paired-end data</b>).</li>
  <li>Inspect the quality control reports produced by nextflow.</li>
  <li>Perform exploratory analysis in R.</li>
  <li>Perform Differential Gene Expression Analysis (DGEA) in R.</li>
  <li>Perform pathway analysis in R.</li>
  <li>Next steps ?</li>
</ol>

# Raw data quality control

## MultiQC
MultiQC is looking generally good with respect to most tests.Sequence duplicattion yellow and red status warnings are raised but these can be expected in RNA-seq. The <b>GC-content</b> plot is one point of concern:

<details><summary>Plot before trimming by trimgalore</summary>
![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/fastqc_per_sequence_gc_content_plot.png")`)
</details>

<ul>
  <li><b>At 60%:</b> The small peaks are COHTN-13, COHTC-58 and COHTN-12.</li>
  <li><b>At 65-70%:</b> Peaks are from COHTN-13, COHTC-16, COHTN-6, COHTN-3, COHTC-58.</li>
</ul>

<details><summary>Plot after trimming by trimgalore</summary>
![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/fastqc_trimmed_per_sequence_gc_content_plot.png")`)
</details>

<ul>
  <li><b>At 60-65%:</b> The small peaks are COHTN-13, COHTC-58 and some more COHTC samples, but with lower peaks.</li>
</ul>

Therefore, quite a few of the normal samples (given their total is 8) look problematic (also in exploratory plots later). 

When looking at over-represented sequences in the multiQC report, the following is highlighted:

1. <b>TCGCACATTCCGCTTCTACCGGGGGGGTCGAGCTGAGTGGATGCGAATCT</b>, 53 samples. This sequence is a synthetic oligonucleotide contaminant (aptamer ‘signaling polynucleotide’), matching [SEQ ID NO: 2 from US 10,344,319 B2](https://patents.google.com/patent/US10344319B2/en). It's most likely a contamination of some kind that is a "no-hit" in FastQC reports.

2. <b>CTGGAGTCTTGGAAGCTTGACTACCCTACGTTCTCCTACAAATGGACCTT</b>, 38 samples. A recurring contaminant/adapter-derived fragment seen across many datasets ([link 1](https://files.ega-archive.org/EGAF00000772066/), [link 2](https://bioinformatics.ccr.cancer.gov/docs/bioinformatics-for-beginners-2025/data/hcc1395_raw_fastqc/hcc1395_tumor_rep1_R1_fastqc.html), [link 3](https://faryabi16.pmacs.upenn.edu/wugb/2023-07-05/accessories/HPAP-103_alpha_107444_FGC2386_s_2_TATGGCAC/HPAP-103_alpha_107444_FGC2386_s_2_TATGGCAC_trimmed_fastqc.html)).

## Kraken2 results
I used the original 80 ``fastq.gz`` files to run Kraken2 on the Galaxy server for taxonomy analysis. Overall, there were 1.6% unclassified reads. When looking at the classified reads, 96.85% are human. The plot below is a bar chart with the most abundant taxa IDs mapped to our sequences across all samples (<b>excluding Homo sapiens which is the dominant</b>). 

![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/taxa_bar_chart.png")`)

Given the above, we proceeded with the downstream analysis, without taking any "correcting" action.

# Exploratory analysis
## Preprocessing
Firstly we import and clean up the raw count files:
<ol>
  <li>We have <b>80 samples</b> for 40 patients (2 per patient).</li>
  <li>Import each sample's ``*quant.sf`` files.</li>
  <li>Use ``tximport`` along with the corresponding ``tx2gene`` files to annotate the transcripts.</li>
  <li>Remove <u>3585/61510</u> (5.83%) features with only zero counts.</li>
  <li>Inspect the samples by generalized PCA and MDS using Poisson distances to see whether samples from the same patient are very similar to each other (with respect to raw counts).
  ![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/dimred_prior_to_sum.png")`)
  </li>
  <li>Samples from the same patient are very similar to each other. We proceed by <b>summing the counts</b> for the samples of each patient. Subsequent <b>normalization</b> in <em>DESeq2</em> will take this into acconut.
  
  <details>
    <summary><u>Resources which justify this approach</u></summary>
      <ul>
        <li>[In Bioconductor](https://support.bioconductor.org/p/85536/)</li>
        <li>[In Bioinfo forum](https://www.seqanswers.com/forum/bioinformatics/bioinformatics-aa/48596-why-sum-technical-replicates-instead-of-averaging-and-rounding-for-deseq?t=60996#4)</li>
        <li>[Biostars, link 1](https://www.biostars.org/p/273421/)</li>
        <li>[Biostars, link 2](https://www.biostars.org/p/9542505/#9542536)</li>
      </ul>
  </details>
  </li>
  <li>We proceed by removing features which don't map to gene symbols <u>OR</u> map to RF* or AF\*.* sequences. Total number of features is reduced to <b>38339</b>.</li>
  <!--<li>We add a <u>final filtering step</u> using the ``filterByExpr()`` function of <em>edgeR</em> to remove genes which do not have "enough statistical power" for differences in recurrence in our data: <b>38339 &#8594; 34049</b> features.</li>-->
</ol>

## Creating the DESeq2 dataset for QC
We used a triple interaction term for the original DESeq dataset. The triple interaction term involves all possible interactions between <b>sample type (tumor/normal), recurrence (recurrence/no recurrence) and binned tumor stage (early/late)</b>. 

<b>This object is used only for the exploratory analysis and not for the actual DGEA.</b>

```{r deseq, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = summed_counts,
                              colData = coldata,
                              design = ~Sample.type*Stage*Recurrence)
```

## Count normalization
In order to normalize the raw counts, we use <em>DESeq2</em>'s approach with ``estimateSizeFactors()`` (also called the geometric mean method). We additionally transform the data by:
<ol>
  <li>adding a <b>pseudocount</b> selected via a [data-driven way](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/404962v1.full) (in our case it is 1)</li>
  <li>$\log_2$-transformation</li>
  <li><b>Standardization</b> (for each feature subtract the mean; divide by st. dev.) is applied later for further plotting</li>
</ol>

## Count density plots
The density curves of the raw counts of each sample (each sample's density curve is drawn with a different color) is shown on the figure below (x-axis is capped at 30). These plots illustrate the frequencies of different count values in samples. We generally see low counts dominating the distributions, as expected in RNA-seq data.

![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/OSCC_filtered_read_counts_color_densities_xlim30.png")`)

The corresponding curves for the $\log_2$-normalized data are shown below.

![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/OSCC_filtered_log2normcounts_color_densities.png")`)

The two plots show that regardless of transformation the samples have similar distributions and no apparent extreme outliers exist.

## Additional exploratory plots
### VST and rlog
<b>Variance-stabilizing transformation (vst)</b> and <b>regularized logarithmic (rlog)</b> transformation are two types of transformation for RNA-seq counts included in DESeq2, to improve visualizations. 
We use both of them here for exploratory purposes, but later on we either use the raw counts or the standardized $\log_2$-transformed data.

![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/meanSdPlot.png")`)

In the plots above, each point represents a feature. The plots illustrate **how** the st.deviation (and by extension the variance) of each feature is affected by the magnitude of the mean value for the same feature (in other words, what's the relationship between variance and mean). This is a known problem in RNA-seq (particularly in raw counts) called <b>overdispersion</b>: the variance of the counts is significantly larger than the mean. Each of these three transformations seeks to circumvent this issue. Each does it to a different degree.

The $\log_2$-transformation is achieving low variance for low counts, lower variance for high counts, but high variance for median counts which is not ideal. The <em>rlog</em> has a few outliers in the high range and more in the mid-range. The <em>vst</em> achieves a smooth transition from low to higher counts.

Below we have three heatmaps which illustrate the expression of the top 50 genes (top 50 highest mean values), for the three different transformations. They are only produced for exploratory purposes. No clear patterns can be found, but that is not necessarily indicative of the relationships between expression and recurrence. The <em>rlog</em> plot is full blue, because of a couple of outliers.

<details><summary>Expand heatmaps</summary>
![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/top50_heatmap_log2(norm.counts+1).png")`)
![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/top50_heatmap_rlog.png")`)
![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/top50_heatmap_vst.png")`)
</details>

### Heatmaps of distances
Higher distance between two samples translates to dissimilarity. Euclidean distances in the case of <em>vst</em>-transformed data and Poisson distances in the case of raw counts were used to get an overview of similarities across samples and create heatmaps. The two distinct distance metrics are used because they are more appropriate for each data type: vst-transformed data are homoskedastic and roughly in $\log2$-scale, so the Euclidean distance is appropriate, while raw counts are assumed to follow a negative binomial distribution for which Poisson distance is more appropriate.

![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/sample_distance_heatmap_vst.png")`)

This plot indicates <u>COHTN-13 is a possible outlier</u>. Otherwise samples are split into two major groups. There is a <b>mix of all three main variables</b> in the first large group (purple square in the left of the plot). In the second smaller group, there is mix of <b>late recurrent samples and early non-recurrent samples</b>, which are <u>almost</u> all tumors.

![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/sample_poisson_distance_heatmap.png")`)

The Poisson distances also split the samples into two groups with similar patterns. There is a <b>mix of all three main variables</b> in the first large group (purple square in the left of the plot). In the second smaller group, there is mix of <b>late recurrent samples and early non-recurrent samples</b>, which are <u>almost</u> all tumors.

<!--Two ways to measure whether the clusterings are similar are the [Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/adjusted-rand-index) and the [Normalized Mutual Information (NMI)](https://course.ccs.neu.edu/cs6140sp15/7_locality_cluster/Assignment-6/NMI.pdf), however, recently [this](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-59073-9) was published and advises against using the NMI especially for larger numbers of groups.-->

A quantitative way to measure whether the clusterings are similar is the [Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/adjusted-rand-index). The ARI between the two groups is <b>~88%</b>, meaning the patterns uncovered by Poisson distance clustering in the raw counts and Euclidean distance clustering in the <em>vst</em>-transformed data are <u>very similar</u>.

### Dimensionality reduction plots
We carry out Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the <em>vst</em>-transformed data and GLM-PCA on the raw counts (we applied GLM-PCA on the raw counts earlier, prior to summing the counts for each sample; this time we apply it on the filtered data, i.e. after we removed the transcripts that did not pass filtering controls). So, plot A is based on the <em>vst</em>-transformed data and plot B on the raw counts.

<b>In the two plots below, we notice a cluster of normal samples at the top which also surrounded by mainly early tumor samples (recurrence varies though). On the left side of plot A (PCA plot), we see the small cluster we saw in the distance heatmap of the <em>vst</em>-transformed data we saw previously.</b>

![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/PCA.png")`)

Similarly, we apply Multi-Dimensional Scaling (MDS) on the <em>vst</em>-transformed data and the raw count data, using the pre-calculated Euclidean and Poisson distances respectively. MDS is using a set of distances to create a low-dimensional coordinate system onto which samples are mapped in a way that maximizes the preservation of the original high-dimensional distances. So, plot A is based on the <em>vst</em>-transformed data and plot B on the raw counts.

![](`r paste0(getwd(),"/png_exploratory/MDS.png")`)

<b>MDS on the <em>vst</em>-transformed data identifies COHTN-13 as a clear outlier (top of plot A). The small second cluster we saw in the sample distance heatmaps of the <em>vst</em>-transformed data is appearing on the bottom left of plot A. No clear separation is shown in plot B, but if we drew a vertical line at MDS1 = -5000, we would separate that second small cluster on the left, with COHTN-13 presumably at the bottom.</b>

# Sample exclusion
Since our questions are tumor-specific, normal samples are only few (8/40 in total) and early stage normal samples are clear outliers (e.g. COHTN-13), <b>we exclude normal samples from the differential expression analysis to avoid additional noise and model destabilization</b>. This makes our results <b>interpretable in the context of tumors only</b>, but it <b>DOES NOT</b> guarantee some of the changes identified could not also be identified in normal samples (had they been included).

<b>We proceed with the 32 tumor samples</b>. The following table shows the distribution of samples per groups.

```{r tumor_sample_distribution, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
tabdf <- data.frame(
  Recurrence = c("No recurrence", "Recurrence"),
  Early = c(9, 7),
  Late = c(8, 8),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(tabdf,
      format = "html", # change to "latex" if knitting to PDF
      booktabs = TRUE,
      align = c("l","r","r"),
      col.names = c("Recurrence", "Early", "Late"),
      escape = FALSE,
      caption = "Recurrence by Stage"
      ) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped","hover","condensed")) %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Stage" = 2), escape = FALSE)
```

# DGEA

## Wald test
We proceeded by building our final <em>DESeq2</em> model using the following formula: ``~ Stage*Recurrence`` which includes recurrence, stage and their interaction.

<details>
  <summary><b>Expand code:</b></summary>
```{r wald, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
# Libraries #####
library(dplyr)
library(DESeq2)
library(tximport)
library(tximeta)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(edgeR)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(ggpubr)
library(cowplot)
library(pheatmap)
library(rcartocolor)
library(viridisLite)
library(vsn)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(tibble)
library(ggrepel)
library(glmpca)
library(openxlsx)
library(PoiClaClu)
library(EnhancedVolcano)
library(genefilter)
library(grid)
library(gridExtra)
library(IHW)
library(ashr)

# Import environment
load("Resources_and_environments/Preprocessing_and_exploratory_analysis.RData")

# Differential Expression #####
# Tumor-only model for contrasts of interest
dds_Wald_filt <- dds[, dds$Sample.type == "Tumor"]
dds_Wald_filt$Stage      <- droplevels(dds_Wald_filt$Stage)
dds_Wald_filt$Recurrence <- droplevels(dds_Wald_filt$Recurrence)

dds_Wald_filt <- estimateSizeFactors(dds_Wald_filt)     # re-estimate on subset
design(dds_Wald_filt) <- ~ Stage * Recurrence
dds_Wald_filt <- DESeq(dds_Wald_filt, test = "Wald")

# using pre-existing size factors
# estimating dispersions
# gene-wise dispersion estimates
# mean-dispersion relationship
# Note: levels of factors in the design contain characters other than
# letters, numbers, '_' and '.'. It is recommended (but not required) to use
# only letters, numbers, and delimiters '_' or '.', as these are safe characters
# for column names in R. [This is a message, not a warning or an error]
# final dispersion estimates
# fitting model and testing
# Note: levels of factors in the design contain characters other than
# letters, numbers, '_' and '.'. It is recommended (but not required) to use
# only letters, numbers, and delimiters '_' or '.', as these are safe characters
# for column names in R. [This is a message, not a warning or an error]
# -- replacing outliers and refitting for 9295 genes
# -- DESeq argument 'minReplicatesForReplace' = 7 
# -- original counts are preserved in counts(dds)
# estimating dispersions
# fitting model and testing
# Note: levels of factors in the design contain characters other than
# letters, numbers, '_' and '.'. It is recommended (but not required) to use
# only letters, numbers, and delimiters '_' or '.', as these are safe characters
# for column names in R. [This is a message, not a warning or an error]

coefNames <- resultsNames(dds_Wald_filt)
coefNames

# [1] "Intercept"                              "Stage_Late_vs_Early"                   
# [3] "Recurrence_Recurrence_vs_No.recurrence" "StageLate.RecurrenceRecurrence"   

# Define contrasts (use the actual interaction name "StageLate.RecurrenceRecurrence")
contrasts <- list(
  tumor_rec_vs_tumor_no_rec = list(
    contrast   = c("Recurrence_Recurrence_vs_No.recurrence", "StageLate.RecurrenceRecurrence"),
    listValues = c(1, 0.5)   # TR vs TNR, equal stage weighting
  ),
  
  late_tumor_rec_vs_early_tumor_rec = list(
    contrast   = c("Stage_Late_vs_Early", "StageLate.RecurrenceRecurrence"),
    listValues = c(1, 1)     # LTR vs ETR
  ),
  
  early_tumor_rec_vs_early_tumor_no_rec = list(
    contrast   = c("Recurrence_Recurrence_vs_No.recurrence"),
    listValues = c(1)        # ETR vs ETNR
  ),
  
  late_tumor_rec_vs_late_tumor_no_rec = list(
    contrast   = c("Recurrence_Recurrence_vs_No.recurrence", "StageLate.RecurrenceRecurrence"),
    listValues = c(1, 1)     # LTR vs LTNR
  )
)

# Get results and perform IHW
results_raw  <- list()   # DESeqResults objects
results_tbls <- list()   # tidy data.frames with padj_ihw
ihw_objs     <- list()   # IHW fit objects (optional to keep)

for (nm in names(contrasts)) {
  cn   <- contrasts[[nm]]$contrast
  vals <- contrasts[[nm]]$listValues
  
  # Build a named numeric contrast vector over all coefficients
  cv <- setNames(rep(0, length(coefNames)), coefNames)
  
  # Sanity check: all requested coef names exist
  miss <- setdiff(cn, names(cv))
  if (length(miss) > 0) stop(sprintf("Contrast '%s' has unknown coefficients: %s",
                                     nm, paste(miss, collapse = ", ")))
  
  cv[cn] <- vals
  
  # Get DESeq2 results WITHOUT independent filtering,
  # since we will do IHW ourselves on pvalue ~ baseMean
  res <- results(dds_Wald_filt,
                 contrast = cv,
                 independentFiltering = FALSE,
                 cooksCutoff = FALSE)
  
  # Tidy table
  deRes <- as.data.frame(res)
  deRes$gene <- rownames(deRes)
  deRes <- deRes[, c("gene","baseMean","log2FoldChange","lfcSE","stat","pvalue","padj")]
  
  # IHW on (pvalue ~ baseMean). Remove NAs first.
  keep <- is.finite(deRes$pvalue) & !is.na(deRes$baseMean)
  ihwRes <- ihw(pvalue ~ baseMean, data = deRes[keep, c("pvalue","baseMean")], alpha = 0.05)
  
  deRes$padj_ihw <- NA_real_
  deRes$padj_ihw[keep] <- adj_pvalues(ihwRes)
  
  # Store
  results_raw[[paste0("res_", nm)]]  <- res
  results_tbls[[paste0("res_", nm)]] <- deRes
  ihw_objs[[paste0("ihw_", nm)]]     <- ihwRes
}

# Rejected null hypotheses in IHW results
lapply(ihw_objs, rejections)
gc()

# Shrinking logFCs
# apeglm_shrunk_results = list() # apeglm does not work with contrasts
# normal_shrunk_results = list() # normal cannot be implemented with interactions designs
ashr_shrunk_results_raw <- list()  # DESeqResults with shrunken LFCs
ashr_shrunk_tbls       <- list()  # data.frames with log2FC_shrunk + padj_ihw retained

for (nm in names(contrasts)) {
  res_nm <- paste0("res_", nm)
  
  # 1) Shrink using the *same* fitted contrast by passing the DESeqResults
  shr <- lfcShrink(dds_Wald_filt, res = results_raw[[res_nm]], type = "ashr")
  
  # 2) Tidy + merge with your IHW table so we preserve pvalue/padj/padj_ihw
  shr_df <- as.data.frame(shr)
  shr_df$gene <- rownames(shr_df)
  shr_df <- shr_df[, c("gene","baseMean","log2FoldChange","lfcSE")]
  
  # keep original names and add a clear column for shrunk LFC
  colnames(shr_df)[colnames(shr_df) == "log2FoldChange"] <- "log2FC_shrunk"
  colnames(shr_df)[colnames(shr_df) == "lfcSE"]          <- "lfcSE_shrunk"
  
  # merge with the IHW-augmented table you already made
  merged <- merge(
    results_tbls[[res_nm]],  # has gene, baseMean, log2FoldChange (MLE), lfcSE, stat, pvalue, padj, padj_ihw
    shr_df[, c("gene","log2FC_shrunk","lfcSE_shrunk")],
    by = "gene",
    all.x = TRUE,
    sort = FALSE
  )
  
  # store
  ashr_shrunk_results_raw[[res_nm]] <- shr
  ashr_shrunk_tbls[[res_nm]]        <- merged
}
```
</details>

This process essentially fits the following model:
$$
\log\bigl(\mu_j\bigr) \;=\; \beta_0 
\;+\; \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}}\cdot I(\mathrm{Recurrence}=\text{Yes})
\;+\; \beta_{\mathrm{Late}}\cdot I(\mathrm{Stage}=\text{Late}) \\
\;+\; \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}\cdot \bigl[I(\mathrm{Recurrence}=\text{Yes}) \times I(\mathrm{Stage}=\text{Late})\bigr].
$$

where:

<ul>
 <li>$\mu_j$ is the expected count for sample $j$ (tumor-only analysis).</li>
 <li>$\beta_0$ is the intercept (reference levels: Recurrence = No, Stage = Early).</li>
 <li>$\beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}}$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{Late}}$ are the main effects for No $\rightarrow$ Yes and Early $\rightarrow$ Late, respectively.</li>
 <li>$\beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}$ is the interaction effect of being both Recurrence = Yes and Stage = Late (relative to the No/Early baseline).</li>
 <li>$I(\cdot)$ is the 0/1 indicator function.</li>
</ul>

We are interested in the following seven comparisons:

1. **Recurrent Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Tumors Overall**  
2. **Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors vs. Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors**  
3. **Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors**  
4. **Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors**  

To build the contrasts for the first four comparisons, we follow the logic below (tumor-only design, no Sample.type term):

1. **Recurrent Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Tumors Overall**:
   - Compare tumors within stage:
     - Early Tumor, Rec=Yes vs Early Tumor, Rec=No
     - Late Tumor, Rec=Yes vs Late Tumor, Rec=No
   - Early Tumor difference:
     $$
     (\beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}}) - (\beta_0) \;=\; \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}}
     $$
   - Late Tumor difference:
     $$
     (\beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{Late}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}) - (\beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{Late}})
     \;=\; \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}
     $$
   - With equal Early/Late weighting (50/50):
     $$
     \frac{\beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}} + \left(\beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}\right)}{2}
     \;=\; \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}} + 0.5\,\beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}
     $$

2. **Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors vs. Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors**:
   - (Late, Rec=Yes) minus (Early, Rec=Yes):
     $$
     (\beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{Late}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}) - (\beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}})
     \;=\; \beta_{\mathrm{Late}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}
     $$

3. **Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors**:
   - (Early, Rec=Yes) minus (Early, Rec=No):
     $$
     (\beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}}) - (\beta_0) \;=\; \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}}
     $$

4. **Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors**:
   - (Late, Rec=Yes) minus (Late, Rec=No):
     $$
     (\beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{Late}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}) - (\beta_0 + \beta_{\mathrm{Late}})
     \;=\; \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes}} + \beta_{\mathrm{RecYes:Late}}
     $$

By performing the corresponding **Wald** tests on these linear combinations, we obtain the **logFC**’s of interest and can identify the significant genes.

For multiple testing correction we use <b>Independent Hypothesis Weighting (IHW)</b> on the raw p-values using the ``baseMean`` as covariate. IHW controls the FDR like Benjamini–Hochberg, but *learns* data-driven weights for hypotheses using an external covariate (e.g., each gene’s mean normalized count, ``baseMean``) that is **independent of the p-value under the null** yet informative for power. This prioritizes tests that are more likely to be detectable and typically yields more discoveries at the same FDR. 

<b>We get 140, 1584, 391 and 825 significant genes respectively.</b>

<!--In RNA-seq, the IHW paper explicitly demonstrates using the mean normalized counts as the covariate and shows increased power, and DESeq2 provides a supported integration (`filterFun = ihw`) for this purpose.-->

## Shrinkage
We use an additional step, which is <b>shrinkage</b>. The logic behind shrinkage is to moderate spuriously large ``logFC``'s particularly for lowly-expressed genes and give more "realistic" estimates, although it might be case that high ``logFC``'s are not necessarily artefacts. Overall, it preserves directionality, while reducing noise.

The step is optional, but <b>we apply it here</b>. The only shrinkage method which can handle interaction designs is the ``ashr`` method ([Ref](https://doi.org/10.1093/biostatistics/kxw041)). Below are the results of shrinkage for the four different comparisons. Shrinkage is achieved to a certain degree in all cases, <b>but does not entirely fix the abnormally high logFC's in lowly-expressed genes</b>.

## Volcano plots
The volcano plots below show differentially expressed genes in each comparison. Red color is used for up-regulated genes, blue color for down-regulated genes. The rest of the colors is used for genes that do not pass the $p_{adj}$-value threshold (0.05) and/or an arbitrary ``logFC`` cutoff of ±1.

The <b>x</b>-axis shows the calculated ``logFC`` of each gene and the <b>y</b>-axis has the $-\log{p_{adj}}$ for the ``logFC`` of each gene.

# Pathways
## Over-representation analysis (ORA)
Over-representation analysis is based only on the overlaps of the user-provided sets of genes with the known biological sets of genes in a knowledge base like <b>Gene Ontology (GO)</b> or <b>KEGG</b>. They <b>do NOT</b> take the ``logFC``'s into account. Nevertheless, we carry out this analysis using <em>clusterProfiler</em> for the following available gene set resources: <b>GO, KEGG, WikiPathways, Reactome, Disease Ontology (DO), Network of Cancer Gene (NCG) and Disease Gene Network (DGN)</b>. The results are stored in the ``Results/Pathways`` folder, under each comparison's directory in the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/sionaris/oscc_seq_rec).

<b>In the following subsections, if you don't see any result, then there are NO significant results.</b>

### Recurrent Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Tumors Overall
```{r auto_TR_vs_TNR_ORA_loop, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = 'asis'}
ora_loop(ora_pathways = pathways, comp = "ashr_TR_vs_TNR")
```
    
### Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors vs. Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors
```{r auto_LTR_vs_ETR_ORA_loop, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = 'asis'}
ora_loop(ora_pathways = pathways, comp = "ashr_LTR_vs_ETR")
```

### Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors
```{r auto_ETR_vs_ETNR_ORA_loop, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = 'asis'}

```

### Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors
```{r auto_LTR_vs_LTNR_ORA_loop, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = 'asis'}

```

## Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)
Gene Set Enrichment Analysis leverages log fold changes to rank genes by expression variation (<b>in all genes; NOT just the significant ones</b>), enabling the detection of coordinated up- or down-regulation in predefined gene sets and providing more nuanced insights than over-representation analysis, which only assesses the enrichment of selected genes without considering their expression levels. We carry out this analysis using <em>clusterProfiler</em> for the following available gene set resources: <b>GO, KEGG, WikiPathways, Reactome, Disease Ontology (DO), Network of Cancer Gene (NCG) and Disease Gene Network (DGN)</b>; same as ORA. The results are stored in the ``Results/Pathways`` folder, under each comparison's directory in the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/sionaris/oscc_seq_rec).

<b>In the following subsections, if you don't see any result, then there are NO significant results.</b>

### Recurrent Tumors vs. Non-Recurrent Tumors Overall
```{r auto_TR_vs_TNR_GSEA_loop, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = 'asis'}
gsea_loop(gsea_pathways = pathways, comp = "ashr_TR_vs_TNR")
```

### Recurrent Late-Stage Tumors vs. Recurrent Early-Stage Tumors
```{r auto_LTR_vs_ETR_GSEA_loop, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = 'asis'}

```

```{r auto_ETR_vs_ETNR_GSEA_loop, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = 'asis'}

```


## Active Subnetwork Enrichment
<em>pathfindR</em> maps each gene’s statistical significance (from a comparison of interest) onto a <b>protein–protein interaction (PIN) network</b> and then searches for "active subnetworks", which are clusters of closely interacting, significantly altered genes. Each subnetwork is tested for pathway enrichment, and the results are aggregated to reveal biologically relevant pathways that are highly supported by <b>both gene-level evidence and interaction data</b>. This approach goes beyond simple gene-count–based methods like Over-Representation Analysis (ORA) by incorporating interaction patterns rather than just whether a gene is in a pathway, and it differs from GSEA by focusing on actual network connectivity rather than only rank-based enrichment. Consequently, pathfindR can highlight disease-associated pathways that may remain undetected when ignoring the crucial contextual relationships among genes. We carry out this analysis using for the following available gene set resources: <b>GO, KEGG, Reactome, BioCarta</b> and the <b>Biogrid PIN</b>. The results are stored in the ``Results/Pathways`` folder, under each comparison's directory in the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/sionaris/oscc_seq_rec).

<b>In the following subsections, if you don't see any result, then there are NO significant results.</b> Pathways in pathfindR <b>can be clustered to create a representative pathway which is summarizing findings in multiple similar pathways</b>. These can be seen in the corresponding "representative" tables.

